Is Potassium Phenoxy Methyl Penicillin included in Schedule T for ASU drugs, and what potency or unit of measurement is specified for it?

Yes. Item 70 of Schedule T lists “Potassium Phenoxy Methyl Penicillin 48 InI…”. The abbreviation “InI” is interpreted in the schedule as International Units (IU), so the schedule records the drug at a potency of 48 IU. This entry confirms that the substance is officially recognised in the Schedule and that the regulatory reference for its strength is 48 IU.

According to the Drugs Rules, 1945, can a professional or a paid individual be considered a “donor” for blood collection?

No. Clause (g) defines a “donor” as “a person who voluntarily donates blood after he has been declared fit after a medical examination, for donating blood, on fulfilling the criteria given hereinafter, without accepting in return any consideration in cash or in kind from any source but does not include a professional or a paid donor.” The definition explicitly excludes professional or paid donors, limiting the term to voluntary, uncompensated donors only.

What is the statutory procedure for the disposal of drugs that have been confiscated under the Act?

According to the provision titled “Procedure for disposal of confiscated drugs,” the Court must first refer the confiscated drugs to the concerned Inspector for a report on whether the drugs meet standard quality or violate any provision of the Act or Rules (para 1). The Inspector, relying on the Government Analyst’s report, determines if the drugs are sub‑standard or non‑compliant (para 2). If the Inspector concludes that the drugs are not of standard quality or contravene the Act/Rules, he reports this to the Court, which then orders the destruction of the drugs. The destruction must be carried out under the Inspector’s supervision and in the presence of any authority specified by the Court.

How should the date format 'dt. 10-4-1964' be read and what is its legal significance?

The abbreviation "dt." stands for "date". The numeric string "10-4-1964" follows the day‑month‑year convention commonly used in Indian legal documents, meaning the 4th day of the 10th month of the year 1964. Therefore, the date is 4 October 1964. The legal significance is that this is the official date on which the notification (No. F. 1‑10/62‑D) was issued; any rights, obligations, or effects created by that instrument are deemed to have commenced on that date unless the instrument itself provides a different commencement provision.

Which specific form must an Inspector use to notify the person from whom a drug sample is taken about the purpose of the test or analysis?

The Inspector must use Form 17 to give written intimation of the purpose for which the drug sample is being taken. This requirement is set out in Section 56, which states: “When an Inspector takes a sample of a drug for the purpose of test or analysis, he shall intimate such purpose in writing in Form 17 to the person from whom he takes it.”

What safety test protocol is mandated for each batch of freeze‑dried Ranikhet Disease Vaccine under the Drugs & Cosmetics Rules Part XVII?

The Rules prescribe a specific safety test for every batch of the freeze‑dried Ranikhet Disease Vaccine. According to clause (c) of the Standards, twelve healthy young chickens (all from the same source) weighing at least 100 g each must be immunised against Ranikhet Disease. Fourteen days later, the birds are tested with the contents of one ampoule suspended in 100 ml of normal saline. Three birds are injected subcutaneously with 0.1 ml (equivalent to ten times the field dose) to confirm the product is free from viruses or organisms of septicaemia disease. Another three birds are injected intratracheally with the same volume and dose to confirm freedom from the virus of infectious laryngotracheitis and similar diseases.

How are records, being a special type of document, required to be controlled under the quality management system?

The Rules state that records are a special type of document and must be controlled in accordance with the requirements given in the ‘control of records’. Additionally, all documents—including records—must be approved, signed, and dated by the appropriate authorised person. Therefore, records must follow the same procedural controls (review, approval, revision tracking, availability, legibility, identification of external origin, and prevention of obsolete use) as other documents, with the added emphasis that they are governed by the specific ‘control of records’ provisions. This is reflected in the text: “Documents required by the quality management system shall be controlled. Records are a special type of document and shall be controlled according to the requirements given in the control of records. Documents shall be approved, signed and dated by the appropriate and the authorised person.”

What sterility testing requirements must viral vaccines meet under the same regulations?

Viral vaccines must undergo a sterility test that complies with the procedures set out in the general monograph on ‘Viral Vaccines’. The text states: “Sterility Test‑ Should comply with the tests for sterility described in the general monograph on ‘Viral Vaccines’.” Therefore, manufacturers must follow the sterility testing methods detailed in that monograph to satisfy the regulatory requirement.

What specific functions does the controller (1105) perform in the method claimed in Blackberry Ltd. v. Controller of Patents & Designs, 2024?

The controller (1105) carries out two distinct functions within the claimed method. First, it categorizes the media files based on the confidence levels assigned to each file, as stated: "categorizing, by the controller (1105), the media files based on the confidence levels of each media file". Second, it applies a comparison of the file sizes of the categorized media files, which is used to determine a portion of the media storage that is available for automatic filling. This comparison acts as a filter for automatically selecting the media files that will be used to fill the device’s storage, as reflected in the passage: "applying a comparison of file sizes of the categorized ... media files, by the controller (1105), ... with respect to a portion of the media storage that is determined to be available for automatic filling, as a filter for automatically selecting the media files to fill the media storage of the device."

What fees are prescribed for testing the mother tincture and its lower potencies under the GMP schedule for ASU drugs?

Section 6 of the Schedule T GMP for ASU Drugs states that fees are levied for the testing of the mother tincture as well as for lower potencies up to 3 × or 100 equivalent. In other words, any analytical or quality‑control test performed on the original mother tincture or on preparations whose potency does not exceed three times the mother tincture strength—or whose dilution is equivalent to a 1:100 ratio—will attract the prescribed testing fee.

What is the testing principle outlined in Schedule T for condom integrity under the GMP guidelines for ASU drugs?

The schedule specifies that the test principle is to inflate a condom of constant length with air and to record both the volume of air introduced and the pressure inside the condom at the exact moment it bursts. This is captured in the text as ‘Inflation of constant length of the condom with air and recording the volume and pressure at the moment of bursting.’

What investigative responsibilities does the examiner have under Section 13(1) to determine anticipation of a claimed invention?

Under Section 13(1) the examiner to whom an application is referred under section 12 must "make investigation for the purpose of ascertaining whether the invention so far as claimed in any claim of the complete specification—(a) has been anticipated by publication before the date of filing of the applicant’s complete specification in any specification filed in pursuance of an application for a patent made in India and dated on or after the 1st day of January, 1912; (b) is claimed in any claim of any other complete specification published on or after the date of filing of the applicant’s complete specification, being a specification filed in pursuance of an application for a patent made in India and dated before or claiming the priority date earlier than that date." In other words, the examiner must search (i) all Indian patent specifications published on or after 1 January 1912 that pre‑date the filing date, and (ii) any later‑published Indian specifications that contain claims overlapping the applicant’s claims and that have an earlier priority date.

What environmental and structural requirements does the GMP schedule impose on the tablet compression area for ASU drugs?

The schedule specifies that the tablet section must be free from dust and floating particles and may be air‑conditioned. Each tablet compression machine must be isolated into its own cubicle and linked to a vacuum dust collector or an exhaust system. Additionally, the tablet production department must be divided into four distinct sections: (a) Mixing, Granulation and Drying, (b) Tablet compression, (c) Packaging (strip/blister machine as required), and (d) Coating (wherever required) (see Section 3 of the document).

Does the adaptive network optimization module described in the disclosure meet the European Patent Convention’s requirement for a technical contribution in a computer‑implemented invention?

Yes. Under EPC Article 52(2) and the case law (e.g., T 258/03), a computer‑implemented invention must produce a further technical effect beyond the normal physical interactions of the computer. The disclosure recites a processing unit communicatively coupled to a network monitoring unit and at least one NIC, with a memory storing executable instructions for an adaptive network optimization module ("e) a memory storing executable instructions for an adaptive network optimization module"). The processing unit, when executing these instructions, "analyze[s] the acquired real‑time network environment data; determine[s] optimal data transmission parameters" and "transmit[s] control commands to the at least one network interface controller to dynamically implement the determined optimal parameters, thereby maintaining a predetermined data throughput and reducing communication latency across the network amidst fluctuating conditions." This functional description shows that the invention actively monitors real‑time network conditions and dynamically adjusts transmission parameters to maintain throughput and lower latency. Such dynamic adaptation provides a concrete technical effect on the network (improved performance and reliability), which satisfies the EPC’s technical contribution requirement for CRIs.

What synonyms are officially recognized for the Infectious Canine Hepatitis Vaccine according to Schedule T GMP for ASU Drugs?

The Schedule T GMP for ASU Drugs explicitly lists two synonyms for the Infectious Canine Hepatitis Vaccine: (i) "Infectious Canine Hepatitis Vaccine (Living)" and (ii) "Canine Hepatitis Cell Culture Vaccine". This is stated in clause 1 of the document, which reads: "Synonyms : Infectious Canine Hepatitis Vaccine (Living), Canine Hepatitis Cell Culture Vaccine."

Does a bio‑informatics data‑processing method, such as the illustrative claim involving chemical substances and vector‑expressed amounts, fall within the Section 3(k) exclusion of mathematical or computer programmes per se?

Section 3(k) expressly excludes "mathematical or business method or a computer programme per se or algorithms" from patentability. The text notes that "Bio‑informatics is a relatively young science and has emerged from the combination of information technology and biotechnology. Thus, the determination of patentability of inventions relating to bioinformatics requires special attention vis‑à‑vis exclusions under Section 3(k) of the Act." The illustrative claim describes a "data processing method" that manipulates chemical substance information and expresses a characteristic amount as a vector. Because the claim is framed purely as a data‑processing algorithm without reciting a technical effect beyond the abstract manipulation of data, it is likely to be caught by the Section 3(k) exclusion. To avoid the exclusion, the claim must be anchored to a concrete technical application (e.g., a specific diagnostic device, a therapeutic formulation, or a tangible biological result) rather than being limited to the abstract computational steps.

I have developed a new pharmaceutical formulation that is just a physical mixture of two known drugs. Can I obtain a patent for this composition under the Indian Patent Act?

No, such a composition is not patentable. Section 3(e) of the Indian Patent Act, as amended by Act 15 of 2005 (effective 1‑1‑2005), expressly excludes "a substance obtained by a mere admixture resulting only in the aggregation of the properties of the components thereof" from patentability. Because your formulation is merely a physical mixture that does not create any new synergistic or unexpected property beyond the sum of its parts, it falls within this exclusion and cannot be granted a patent.

If a pharmaceutical product is manufactured on 1 January 2024, by what date must its expiry be set according to the Rules?

The expiry must be set no later than sixty months after the manufacturing date. Sixty months from 1 January 2024 is 1 July 2029. Therefore, the product’s expiry date must be on or before 1 July 2029, in compliance with clause 9 of the Rules which limits the expiry to "Not exceeding sixty (60) months from the date of manufacture."

Are there any situations where the prior‑approval requirement of Section 4 does not apply to the dissemination of research findings?

Yes. The amendment provides an explicit carve‑out: "Provided that the provisions of this section shall not apply if publication of National Biodiversity research papers or dissemination of knowledge in any seminar or workshop involving the Authority." Therefore, publishing research in National Biodiversity papers or presenting it at seminars or workshops that involve the Authority is exempt from the prior‑approval mandate.

Is it required to provide the names of technical staff on the licence document for Ayurvedic/Siddha/Unani drug manufacturing, and what is the purpose of this requirement?

Yes, the document explicitly includes a line titled "Names of technical staff," indicating that the licence must list the qualified technical personnel responsible for the manufacturing process. This requirement ensures that the regulatory authority can verify that the facility is staffed by individuals with the appropriate expertise, which is a condition for compliance under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules 1945. Failure to include these names could result in the licence being considered incomplete or non‑compliant, potentially leading to suspension or denial of renewal.

What validation procedures are required for filling machines under the GMP schedule for ASU drugs?

Section 7.3 of the schedule requires that filling machines be challenged initially and then at periodic intervals by simulation trials that include a sterile media fill. Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and acceptance criteria for these media fills must be established, justified and documented. For special products such as ophthalmic ointments, special simulation‑trial procedures must also be developed, validated and documented.

What post‑marketing surveillance (PMS) documentation is required for a drug and how long must it be retained?

The regulations require that details of the PMS study report be maintained for the marketing period, but the period must not exceed five years. This is captured in clause 2.18: "Details of PMS study report for marketing period not exceeding five years."

What is the significance of Notification No. F‑18‑1/46 dated 18‑6‑48 in the context of the Drugs Rules 1945?

The citation ‘Renumbered by Notification No. F‑18‑1/46, dt. 18‑6‑48’ indicates that the specific rule (or provision) in the Drugs Rules 1945 was assigned a new numerical identifier by an official government notification issued on 18 June 1948. The notification (F‑18‑1/46) does not alter the substantive content of the rule; it merely updates its numbering to align with a revised schedule or to correct earlier numbering inconsistencies. Consequently, any reference to that rule after the date of the notification should use the new number as prescribed in Notification F‑18‑1/46.

How does the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules define “Streptococcus equi Vaccine”?

The Rules define Streptococcus equi Vaccine as “a phenolised culture of a number of different isolates of Streptococcus equi in glucose serum broth.” This definition specifies three essential elements: (i) the vaccine must be a culture that has been phenolised, (ii) it must contain multiple distinct isolates of the bacterium Streptococcus equi, and (iii) the culture medium used is glucose serum broth.

What documentation is required from a manufacturer concerning the test protocol of a diagnostic kit under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules Part XVI?

The manufacturer must submit a test protocol that clearly shows the specifications of the kit and the method of testing. In addition, an in‑house evaluation report covering the kit’s sensitivity, specificity and stability studies must be provided. This requirement is stated in the rule: “Test protocol of the kit showing the specifications and method of testing. In house evaluation report of sensitivity, specificity and stability studies carried out by the manufacturer.”

According to the Drugs Rules 1945, what types of vessels are authorized for use in the preparation of Lavana Bhasma Satva?

The rule explicitly lists the vessels that may be used for preparing Lavana Bhasma Satva. The excerpt states: "Lavana Bhasma Satva / /patila flask, Multani Matti / Plaster" and also mentions "stainless steel vessels" earlier in the same line. Therefore, both stainless steel vessels and traditional containers such as a patila (metal pot), Multani Matti (a type of clay), and plaster are permissible under the Rules for this preparation.

Under Section 87, what conditions must be satisfied before the Controller can order the grant of a licence for a related patent?

The Controller may only make an order granting a licence for a related patent if two conditions are met: (i) the applicant must be able and willing to grant, or procure the grant of, a licence in respect of the other invention to the patentee and his licensees (if they so desire) on reasonable terms; and (ii) the licence must be granted on reasonable terms. This is expressly stated in the text: “No order under such an application shall be made unless the Controller is satisfied – i. that the applicant is able and willing to grant, or procure the grant to the patentee and his licensees if they so desire, of a licence in respect of the other invention on reasonable terms; and ii.”

What is the appeal process for a person aggrieved by a suspension or cancellation order of an import licence, and within what time limit must the appeal be filed?

The text provides that an aggrieved person may appeal to the Central Government within thirty days of receiving the order. The Central Government will then conduct an enquiry as it considers necessary, give the appellant an opportunity to present his views, and subsequently pass any orders it deems appropriate. This right and timeframe are detailed in the provision following clause 4[29] and reiterated in clause 3[29A].

What Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) obligations apply to the production of Potassium Phenoxy Methyl Penicillin under the Schedule T provisions?

Because Potassium Phenoxy Methyl Penicillin appears in Schedule T (see entry 70), it is subject to the same GMP requirements that apply to every drug listed in the schedule. Specifically, manufacturers must: (i) obtain a licence under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act; (ii) maintain validated manufacturing processes that ensure the drug’s potency of 48 IU as stated; (iii) implement quality‑control testing for identity, purity, and potency in accordance with the schedule’s specifications; (iv) keep complete batch records and conduct regular internal audits; and (v) submit periodic compliance reports to the licensing authority. These obligations are derived directly from the Schedule T framework, which mandates that all listed ASU drugs, including Potassium Phenoxy Methyl Penicillin, be produced in GMP‑compliant facilities.

Can I include non‑English technical terms and informal language in the description of my patent application, or are there specific language requirements?

Clause e) of the Manual states that any terms in other languages used in the description must be accompanied by their English equivalents. Moreover, the use of vague words, slang, and colloquialisms is expressly described as "objectionable and shall be avoided." Consequently, you must provide an English translation for every foreign‑language term and ensure that the description uses precise, formal language without slang or ambiguous expressions.

Does the public display of an invention at an industrial exhibition, with the consent of the true and first inventor, constitute anticipation under Section 31?

No. Section 31(d) expressly states that an invention shall not be deemed to have been anticipated "by reason only of the display of the invention with the consent of the true and first inventor… at an industrial or other exhibition" to which the provisions of the section have been extended by the Central Government. Therefore, a consensual display at a notified exhibition does not count as anticipation.

What are the mandatory elements of a routine sanitation program for a drug manufacturing premises under the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules?

Section 9.3 of the Rules requires that a routine sanitation program be drawn up, observed, and properly recorded. The program must specify (a) the specific areas to be cleaned and the cleaning intervals, (b) the cleaning procedure to be followed, including the equipment and materials to be used for cleaning, and (c) the personnel assigned to and responsible for the cleaning operation. This ensures that the premises remain free from waste, dust, debris, and other contaminants as mandated in 9.1.

What elements are required in the description of a quality control system for ASU drugs as per Schedule T?

Clause 29.8 (Quality Control) of Schedule T mandates that the applicant provide: (a) a "description of the quality control system and of the activities of the Quality Control Department," and (b) "Procedures for the release of the finished products." This means the submission must outline the organisational structure of the QC department, the specific testing and analytical methods employed, sampling plans, criteria for acceptance/rejection, and the step‑by‑step process that governs the final release of each batch of finished product.

Does the described method satisfy the requirement of a technical contribution under Indian patent law, making it eligible for patent protection?

Yes. The method involves a technical process performed by a device (210) and its controller (1105): (i) providing a confidence level for each media file, (ii) using that confidence level—a quantitative measure of likeability—to automatically select media files, and (iii) storing the selected files in an allocated amount of storage medium (lines 1‑12). This sequence of data processing, decision‑making, and storage management constitutes a technical effect in the realm of device operation, thereby meeting the technical contribution criterion for patentability in India.

How long does a Geographical Indication registration remain in force, and what are the renewal provisions under the Act?

According to Chapter III, a GI registration is valid for ten years from the date of registration (see Section 13(1)). The registration may be renewed for successive periods of ten years each, provided the holder pays the prescribed renewal fee before the expiry of the current term (Section 13(2)). The renewal application must be filed in the form specified by the Registrar, and upon acceptance, the renewed registration continues to enjoy the same protection as the original term.

Is a patent claim that merely takes advantage of a drop in production cost for a known material or process considered to involve an inventive step?

No. According to point (ii) of the text, "It is also not inventive to respond to a change in economic circumstances; for example if a product has not been made from a particular material or by a particular process for reason of cost, and the material or process becomes cheaper or the market value of the product increases, it is not inventive to take advantage of this." Therefore, exploiting a cheaper material or process alone does not satisfy the inventive‑step requirement.

Is the Controller obligated to give the other grantees or the person in default an opportunity to be heard before issuing directions under Section 51?

Yes. Before the Controller issues any directions pursuant to an application under Section 51, the law mandates that the Controller must give an opportunity to be heard to the other person or persons registered as grantee or proprietor of the patent, or to the person in default. The text states: “Before giving any directions in pursuance of an application under this section, the Controller shall give an opportunity to be heard to the other person or persons registered as grantee or proprietor of the patent or to the person in default.”
